content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper "Correspondences between word learning in children and captioning models" investigates the parallels between accuracy at a an image captioning task by artificial neural networks, and the language acquisition process of young children. In particular it analyzes the correlation between performance on the COCO image captioning task with the "age of acquisition" (AoA). They explore this question using a number of different neural architectures (pretrained/non-pretrained, classifiers/generators, LSTMs/Transformers), and find that there is a fairly consistent correlation between the two, which remains even after controlling for word frequency. They find that this correlation can be largely explained by the mutual correlation of SPICE/AUC and AoA with a word's concreteness, which when added to the regression, renders the accuracy of the neural network in predicting the AoA non-significant.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- Paper was clearly written with no obvious typos. I had no difficulty in understanding the findings.

- Paper performed follow-up analyses to check for confounding variables.

- Paper examined several different neural architectures, including training their own from scratch.


Weaknesses:

- Introducing the raw counts as an independent variable in the regression analysis is naive, since these span several orders of magnitude, as can be seen in Figure 4a. It would make more sense to sqrt-transform the counts first. This could very well affect the conclusion drawn in Table 3.

- The authors did not investigate their conclusions on any architectures which have achieved SOTA performance on the COCO image-captioning task, even though many of them are open-source (see https://paperswithcode.com/sota/image-captioning-on-coco-captions).

- In this reviewer's opinion, the main benefit of training new non-SOTA networks on this task would have been to explore how their performance on particular words/categories changed over the course of training, which could have led to a measure similar to AoA, but for the networks themselves. This seems like a natural line of inquiry that is missing from the paper.

- The listed AUC values for the two ResNet classifiers are clustered tightly around 0.5, (range ~0.46-0.54), which is chance performance. This calls into question how well these networks are able to do the task at all.

- The decision to only consider inter-category relationships significantly weakens the conclusions of the paper. The authors state that this was done "because the mismatch between the distributions of COCO and child-directed speech is more substantial at the level of individual words than at the level of word categories". As the authors themselves point out, aggregating at the category level only partially alleviates this, as can be seen in Figure 3 which shows that 'locations' and 'quantifiers' make up the considerable majority of all COCO training data. Therefore it would make more sense to compare subsets of the words from the TalkBank and COCO datasets to which the children and models had the most comparable levels of exposure. This could be done by, for example, keeping only those words which had similar relative frequencies within the two datasets, and discarding others.

- The authors' statement that they aggregated at the word category level "In order to compare word learning at scale" leans overly on buzzwords, and should be rewritten or removed.

- The overall thesis of the paper (that SPICE/AUC correlate strongly with AoA) is significantly diluted by the confounding variable of concreteness, which is found to be strongly correlated with both AoA and SPICE. If it is in fact true that the correlation between SPICE/AUC and AoA is almost entirely mediated by concreteness, then the paper should be centered around deeper exploration of this fact, rather then leaving it off until the final subsection of the Results. Moreover, the high correlation of this concreteness measure with the trained neural models might itself be an artifact of the fact that the concreteness values from Köper & im Walde (2017) were themselves generated by training a neural network on word-embeddings, which were themselves learned by yet another network. In other words, these image-captioning scores might be strongly correlated with this measure of concreteness because both are generated by neural network models of language.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper was easy to read and understand. The question it was exploring (the relation between performance of neural captioning models and AoA in children) was straightforwardly presented, as were its series of analyses exploring potential confounder variables. The writing was clear, concise, and devoid of typos.

Quality: The paper had a number of technical weaknesses (near-chance level AUCs, lack of count-data transformation prior to running linear regression, heavy confounding by concreteness), and a number of natural avenues of inquiry left unexplored (performance on non-aggregated word data, performance of neural networks over the course of training, deeper exploration into the relationship with concreteness, performance of any SOTA image-captioning models from the past 5 years), that significantly detracted from the overall quality.

Novelty: The overall direction of exploring human language acquisition through the lens of artificial neural networks is not new (Tikkala 1998, Shain & Elsner 2020), however this paper's approach of doing so by leveraging large datasets from both the human and NN side (TalkBank and COCO) might well be. However as mentioned in the quality section, there are many additional experiments that the authors could have performed, but didn't, which diminishes the overall novelty of the paper.

Reproducibility: The authors use fairly standard data, network components, and statistical analyses within their paper, which significantly helps with reproducibility. However they could do more by open-sourcing their training and analysis code, and linking it within the paper. They could also be more rigorous in their description of how they computed their word-level and category-level AUC and SPICE scores.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper "Correspondences between word learning in children and captioning models" was a well-written exploration of the relationship between the performance of neural networks on an image captioning task compared to the age-of-acquisition of various words in children. Although the paper examines a number of different neural networks, and performs a number of regression analyses, the overall conclusions of the paper are rather weak. The main finding is that models trained for image captioning on COCO have a per-word-category SPICE score that is significantly correlated with both TalkBank AoA and a measure of concreteness. However neither of these findings is surprising, and moreover the correlation with concreteness is so strong that it explains almost the entirety of the correlation with with AoA. Due to the lack of technical contribution and weak empirical findings, I recommend that this paper be rejected. To meet the bar for acceptance it would need to address the technical shortcomings and perform the follow-up experiments described in the "Weaknesses" and "Quality" sections. It would also need a more coherent thesis around what the paper is purporting to show that is novel/surprising/technically-interesting, rather than the high-level takeaway of "neural network image captioning performance is correlated with AoA, and this can be almost entirely explained by their mutual correlation with concreteness".

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper investigates whether a human can capture the visual difficulty of learning words by examining the image caption model performance. Specifically, they verify the models for different categories of words and examine the correspondence to children's word learning. It starts from the finding that the performance of captioning models correlates with human judgments of words. These findings suggest that models capture the complex real-world association between words and image content. Their findings provide some insights into child development.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The detailed implementation of those models should be described in this paper. Also, they mentioned open-source; providing the link to those codes is necessary to reproduce the results.

The ablation study part is weak, and they select SPICE as the target metric for caption evaluation, while as complementary, Adopting the CIDEr score should also be considered. 

Fig 2 is hard to read out and understand; those figures are put together and make the reader hard to follow.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is hard to follow, and the contribution is limited.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this study, the researchers studied how to capture the visual difficulty of learning words by evaluating the performance of image captioning models, and to compare these models to real world acquisition data from child development. To do this, they took two datasets: WordBank (a child language database) and the COCO dataset and trained several models to caption an image. The labels for the image were derived from the COCO dataset as well as WordBank. First, the researchers trained/tested their models on this task using different combinations of computer vision models and NLP models comparing SPICE and AUC to the Age of Acquisition, which is the median age at which children acquire a word. This score is used to quantify the “difficulty” of learning a word. Paper found a statistically significant correlation of SPICE and AUC to the age of acquisition. Next, the researchers completed a multiple regression analysis on the models using the TalkBank word frequency in addition to SPICE and AUC. It also found a statistically significant correlation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
+ Novel use of datasets and modes comparing machine learning to child development, suggesting new ways to synthesize machine learning with child development.
+ Provides recommendations for developmental psychologists on the use of machine learning to study word acquisition in children.
+ The use of “concreteness” vs “abstractness” of a category was interesting as an additional level of analysis for the study. This is something that could provide future collaborations between developmental linguists and computer scientists in studying child development.

Weaknesses:
- While the paper poses an interesting question, it does not go into sufficient depth to advance the science. There is no clear hypothesis connecting neural networks and child development and the results and discussion of the results do not reveal many useful insights. 
- It is not quite clear why would a difficulty neural networks have in learning to recognize different concepts from images be related with how toddles learn words. There are too many steps to establish this connection and the paper fails to establish the connection. Rather, the possible connection is considered at a superficial level. 
- The researchers state “Developmental scientists have not formulated how the infant mind may process and represent the statistics of visual scenes and labels. Moreover, little is known about how this process may shape word learning.” This paper is missing key research on relational frame theory by Hayes et. al., that describes how some of these processes occur.
- It is unclear why age of acquisition is the dependent variable as a measure of difficulty. The researchers state that they are using this based on research regarding calculation of a child’s difficulty in learning to read a word but reading a word and captioning an image (by saying it) are two different skills. 
- This study trained models to identify categories of words, rather than individual words. The age of acquisition score would calculate the learning of the individual word. The connection between model scores and child age of acquisition as a variable with this study is unclear.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: 4/5 — The paper was easy to follow.
Reproducibility: 4/5 — The description of models and parameters was clear.
Novelty: 3/5—The idea is interesting.
Quality: The paper does not go into sufficient depth to explore the original insight..
content.summary_of_the_review: The papers aimed to explore connections between developmental psychology and deep learning. While the premise is interesting and certainly wort exploring, the paper does not go into sufficient depth to obtain useful insights.
